### Reviewer 1

This manuscript cannot be accepted for publication in any Journal. The quantum dots used for this study have not been characterized to any extent and there are huge flaws in the materials section. In addition, since no structural details are given for these CQDs, it is difficult to understand how the authors can claim the “structural evolution” in the title.
In general, the authors try to describe a strategy for the detection and treatment of senescent cells using quantum dots (C3N QDs). The authors used machine learning to define the structural properties of these carbon nanoparticles, specifically designed to have photodynamic activity. The paper explains how the QDs selectively interact with cellular environments based on NAD+ concentration, allowing for fluorescent detection of senescent cells (which have lower NAD+ levels) and targeted elimination through photodynamic therapy. The approach used is validated in vitro and in animal studies, demonstrating some potential for addressing aging-related pathologies. In addition, the interactions between C3N QDs and NAD+ have been studied using density functional theory (DFT) calculations, but there is nothing in the manuscript about how these calculations were performed.
Unfortunately, this work presents several inconsistencies, mainly concerning the material preparation and characterization. I believe that for the publication in any journal, several points should be carefully addressed and solved before considering the work.
In general the text is quite confusing and not scientifically acceptable. Other examples of nanodots or particles for the same scopes should be reported, to better describe the framework of interest for the materials prepared. Furthermore, the verb “decline” is used several times in the text in the sense of “decrease”. I don’t find it fitting the scientific context so I suggest substituting it with another verb. There are several assumptions not justified by the experiments.
Here is a list of aspects to be answered.
1) The synthesis reported in the supporting information does not match the one described in the text. Are the dots obtained from m-phenylenediamine and pyrocatechol or from 2,3-Diaminophenazine? Is the reaction done in autoclave? Have the nanoparticles been purified? These aspects should be corrected and clarified. Without the right description of the synthetic procedure, the characterizations reported lose some of their validity.
2) The authors should explain better the reason behind the choice of the two precursors. Assuming that m-phenylenediamine and pyrocatechol have been selected, as stated in the main text, how the two molecules are supposed to react with each other to form the carbon quantum dots? If the reactivity of the reagents is considered, it does not seem that they are chemically compatible (an aromatic amine and a phenolic compound). Is there any specific reason for the choice of those precursors? The nanoparticles synthesis should be better described to highlight the application sections.
3) As reported previously, (DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpcc.0c06996) m-phenylenediamine, and its structural isomers, are known for giving fluorescent side products that alter the emission properties of the final dots, ending up in imaginative results. In many cases, the use of m-phenylenediamine affords green emitting mixtures of low fluorescent carbonaceous particles and green emitting molecules. The emitting species absorb in the UV region of the spectra, close to 250 – 280 nm. Similar absorption band can be seen in the UV-spectra of the nanomaterials reported by the authors in Supplementary Figure 4. This aspect has strong implications in the reliability of the materials obtained. The authors should validate their material, by checking its composition, describe the right synthetic procedure and validate the absence of fluorescent impurities that may rule the nanomaterials fluorescence (or general properties). I suggest at least carrying out mass spectroscopy experiments, to evidence any molecular impurities.
4) In Supplementary Fig. 2 only one particle is shown for the HR-TEM. Anyway, the analysis of only one particle is not enough to define the overall crystallinity of the materials. Furthermore, crystallinity may arise from experimental conditions, such as the exposure of the nanoparticles to high voltage beam during the experiments. In other word, the crystallinity of only one particle cannot reflect the features of the bulk material. HR-TEM should be implemented with images of other nanoparticles and the morphological data should be supported with X-Ray diffraction on powder to confirm the nano- and bulk crystalline feature.
5) The purification of dots is a current topic in the scientific community (https://doi.org/10.1002/smll.202206714; 10.1039/C9NR01029G). Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy is a helpful technique to assess the purity and composition of the dots. In particular, molecular impurities appear in the spectrum as sharp peaks, peaks, while the protons of the nanoparticles give broad and enlarged signals (DOI: 10.1002/anie.202200038). Before any applications, the nanomaterials should be characterized by means of proton NMR spectroscopy and DOSY analysis to precisely describe their composition and the water diffusion coefficient (that should be lower than that of the precursors or small molecules in general) comparing the results with those of the precursors. The materials used for biological experiments should be exhaustively characterized. This is a golden rule in science.
6) Fluorescence is exploited for the quantum dots activity in vitro and in vivo. Anyway, only the UV-vis absorption spectrum is shown in the text, and no emission/fluorescence spectra are reported. Is it well known that carbon quantum dots should be characterized by a wavelength dependent fluorescence, otherwise the presence of fluorescent molecular impurities can be inferred. The authors should address this aspect.
7) For the photodynamic characterization, a laser emitting at 365 nm is selected. Anyway, in clinical applications- or biomedical publications- lasers at lower wavelength are used, since high energy sources can be cause of damage. This decreases a lot the interest for these materials in PDT.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript entitled “Structural evolution of carbon frameworks realizes in vitro interfacial transport in metabolically reprogrammed senescent cells for senolysis”, reported that nitrogen doping in graphene quantum dots (GQDs) is a factor determining their photodynamic properties, a conclusion supported by a machine learning model. The authors extend this finding to discuss the related photodynamic characteristics of C3N quantum dots (QDs). A key finding is that the fluorescence of C3N QDs taken up by cells changes depending on the intracellular NAD+ concentration, enabling the distinction between normal and senescent cells. Furthermore, the study challenged to reveals that subsequent laser irradiation endows these C3N QDs with senolytic activity.
While C3N QDs show potential as a senolysis, the in vivo experiments presented in Figure 6 lack a comparison between healthy controls and the senescence model. Additionally, the assessment of cellular senescence in the in vivo context is insufficient. Therefore, the establishment and validation of the cellular senescence models used throughout the manuscript require careful verification.
Regarding the diabetic ulcer model, the specific mouse model used is not described, and it is unclear whether the model was properly established. The lack of appropriate healthy controls precludes interpretation of the results of this study. Finally, the description of the cell lines used in various experiments is often unclear, making it difficult to assess the consistency and coherence of the experiments.
Detailed points regarding necessary revisions and additional data are listed below.
Major Comments
1. Senescent cells may undergo apoptosis or necrosis due to prolonged laser irradiation, independent of any photodynamic activity. Please provide data on the biosafety of laser irradiation alone on senescent cells to rule out this possibility. While the in vivo data in Figure 6 suggests that irradiation alone does not reduce senescent cells, specific data for the in vitro model in Figure 5a is crucial to confirm this.
2. In figure 6 and related supplementary figures, the "Control" group in these figures appears to be the senescence-induced mouse model. However, data from a healthy, age-matched control group is missing. The authors must show that senescence markers (e.g., β-gal staining, p16/p21 expression) are significantly elevated in the senescence model compared to the healthy controls to validate the model's phenotype. Similarly, for the diabetic mouse model, data demonstrating delayed wound healing compared to healthy control mice is required to establish the model's validity.
3. Most of the experiment rely on experiments using HUVECs. The induction of senescence in these cells should be confirmed at the protein level, in addition to the currently presented data.
Minor Comments
1. Figure 1e, In the top-left panel, the color-coding for the percentages (red and blue) appears to be reversed in the pie chart. Please check and correct it. In the left most graph of the third row, there are no data dots plotted. Please clarify if this is intentional or a plotting error.
2. Figure 2d and Page 6, Lines 34-36, The figure includes shaded areas representing the NAD+ concentration ranges for "Senescent cell" and "Healthy cell." However, the data supporting these specific ranges is not provided or cited. Please provide the evidence for these ranges.
3. Figure 2h, Figure 3a-c, and Supplementary Figs. 7, 31, Please specify the cell types and the methods used to induce senescence for the experiments shown in these figures.
4. Page 6, Line 15, The text states, "Error bars in (g) and (i) indicate the SD of three repetitive tests." This appears to be a typo. Should "(i)" be "(h)"?
5. Figure 3a, At the 48-hour time point, the PL intensity in the senescent cell homogenate is comparable to that of normal cells. Why does it not show the expected decrease? Is it possible that NAD+ was removed or diluted during the homogenization process, thereby eliminating its fluorescence quenching effect? Please clarify.
6. Figure 4g, The methodology for measuring the PL intensity in serum samples (e.g., the concentration of C3N QDs added, incubation time) is not described. Please add these experimental details.
7. Figure 5, The Methods section lacks details regarding the RNA-sequencing experiment. Please provide a comprehensive description of the library preparation, sequencing, and data analysis pipelines.
8. Page 13, Lines 28 & 30, The text provides numerical values for changes in fluorescence intensity and cell proliferation. Please specify which cell line these numbers refer to.
9. Page 13, Lines 30 & 32, The figure citations appear to be incorrect. Should "Fig. 5d–g" be "Fig. 5d–f" and "Fig. 5h and i" be "Fig. 5g and h"? Please verify.
10. Terminology on Pages 13-14, The term "aging marker" is used frequently. In the context of induced senescence, "senescence marker" would be a more precise and appropriate term. Please consider revising the terminology.
11. Figure 6, The manuscript lacks crucial details about the in vivo experimental procedures. Please add a thorough description of the methods, including: how the aged/senescent mice were generated, the parameters for laser irradiation (e.g., area, duration), the strain of diabetic mice used, the procedure for wound creation, and the exact timing of sacrifice.
12. Figure 6, The mouse model used in Figure 6 appears to be a model of induced senescence (e.g., doxorubicin-induced) rather than a model of natural aging. Please revise the terminology throughout the manuscript for accuracy.
13. Page 15, Lines 21 & 23, The term "swelling" is used to describe the wound. Please clarify what this refers to. Does it mean inflammation or the formation of granulation tissue?
14. Figure 6k and 6m, Please provide a description of the methods used for the quantification of the unhealed wound distance and collagen content.
15. Page 15, Line 29, The manuscript claims, “Additionally, the dermis layer and hair follicles rapidly returned to normal.” This is a strong statement, as it is generally understood that severe dermal injury leads to scar formation, which replaces normal dermal structures, including hair follicles. If true tissue regeneration with de novo hair follicle formation occurred, this is a significant finding that requires substantial evidence. Please provide the evidence supporting this claim. Otherwise, please revise the statement to more accurately describe the observed histology, which likely involves wound contraction and re-epithelialization over a scar.
16. Supplementary Figures 7, 10-14, 16, 30, 32, 36, Please state the number of biological samples (n) or experimental replicates for each experiment shown in these figures.
17. Supplementary Figure 14, The figure legend lists series of percentages: "(a) 98.2%, 81.4%, 70.5%, 63.4%, 51.0%. (b) 99.8%, 93.5%, 91.0%, 81.4%, 79.6%." Please clarify what these values represent. Also, please specify if different cell types were used for panels (a) and (b).
18. Supplementary Figure 32, The label "A549" appears to be missing from the top of the corresponding graph. Please correct this.

reviewer_updating.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

Integrating the diagnostic and therapeutic functions of drugs poses challenges due to specific structural design requirements. However, the trial-and-error dilemma in performance-driven structural evolution of nanomaterials is unsatisfactory. Here, we propose a strategy using graphene quantum dots with sp2–sp3 hybridized carbon frameworks for visualized, intelligent targeted clearance of metabolically reprogrammed senescent cells. We establish a structure-activity relationship between the complex nanostructures and photochemical reactivity. We show that property descriptor-based machine learning promotes the evolution of carbon nanostructures, endowing them with exceptionally high photodynamic efficiency. These machine-learning results also guide the design of carbon-based photo/electrocatalytic structures. By examining the interfacial transport properties of in situ carbon nanostructures in excited states, we identify changes in fluorescence and photodynamic activity of C3N quantum dots within metabolically reprogrammed cellular microenvironments. This allows fluorescence detection technology for senescent cells based on C3N quantum dots and an intelligent targeted clearance treatment plan.

---

## Introduction

Achieving integrated diagnosis and therapy for senescent cells is pivotal in addressing aging-related pathologies. A fundamental premise for designing drug structures tailored for dual diagnosis and therapy applications entails the integration of diagnostic and therapeutic functionalities within the drug’s structure based on specific cellular environments 1,2. However, both diagnosis and treatment impose specific structural requirements on drug designs, including different targets 3 and half-lives 4. Meanwhile, the complex interactions between these requirements lead to potential antagonism or synergy 5,6. For example, in the treatment of metabolic reprogramming-related diseases including senescence, when identification and clearance of metabolically reprogrammed cells are required, and when diagnostic and therapeutic functions are based on different targets 7-9, it becomes difficult to achieve an optimal balance between diagnostic accuracy and therapeutic efficacy. Recently, machine learning has demonstrated substantial advantages in elevating the efficiency of drug screening 10,11. However, the black-box dilemma encountered in machine learning (explaining the interfacial physico-chemical mechanisms behind the machine learning structure) makes it difficult to address the need for a comprehensive, holistic understanding of drug design mechanisms 12. Thus, using machine learning to improve the design efficiency of integrated diagnosis and treatment drugs, while simultaneously advancing our understanding of the interfacial physico-chemical mechanisms of drugs in both in vivo and in vitro environments, represents a critical challenge currently confronting scientists 13.

On the other hand, the structurally diversified sp2–sp3 hybrid carbon nanostructures (such as nanodiamonds, carbon dots, graphene quantum dots (QDs), and carbon nanotubes) bring unlimited possibilities for the structural design of integrated diagnosis and treatment drugs targeting metabolic reprogramming-related diseases 14. Whether it is the basic properties of carbon nanostructures (optical properties, electrical properties) or biological effects, extensive discussions have been conducted with the aid of machine learning 11,15. However, it is worth noting that machine learning also faces the common black-box problems in the research into properties of carbon nanostructures 16. More importantly, traditional studies of the structure-activity relationship are insufficient when addressing the complexities of sp2–sp3 hybridized carbon nanostructures 17. Therefore, starting from the structure of integrated diagnosis and treatment drugs, taking carbon nanostructures as the research object explaining the interfacial physico-chemical mechanisms behind machine learning are of significance for simultaneously advancing the understanding of drug action mechanisms 18 and the structure-activity relationship of carbon nanostructures 19.

Here, by combining machine learning with in situ research techniques of solid-liquid interfaces within cells, the selective physicochemical responses of carbon nanostructures are described at interfaces in complex cellular microenvironments. With the assistance of the NMR relaxometry, we elucidate the unique excited-state interfacial transport mechanism in carbon frameworks that underlies the structure-activity relationship. More importantly, we achieve in situ observation of the interfacial transport behaviors of nanostructures within metabolically reprogrammed cellular environments. This research also demonstrates that C3N QDs, characterized by their orderly arranged lattice nitrogen atoms, alter the fluorescence and photodynamic activity across various cell metabolisms. In the microenvironment of metabolically reprogrammed senescent cells, C3N QDs show a low fluorescence intensity and a high photodynamic activity. In contrast, in normal cells, these C3N QDs exhibit increased fluorescence compared to those in aging cells, while their photodynamic activity is suppressed. Such a selective behavior facilitates the targeted elimination of aging cells and enables effective fluorescent labeling of these cells. The reliability of C3N QDs has been confirmed through extensive testing conducted at the cellular, animal, and clinical sample levels.

---

## Results

The structural evolution of a carbon framework
Nitrogen-doped graphene quantum dots (N-GQDs) were prepared through the hydrothermal treatment by using m-phenylenediamine and pyrocatechol as precursors (Supplementary Data 1). The average size of N-GQDs is 6.1 nm (Supplementary Fig. 1). The typical graphene structure of N-GQDs can be observed in Supplementary Fig. 2. Indeed, the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy results indicate that most N atoms exist as lattice-doped N atoms (N–(C)3: 71.4%, C–NH–C: 22.9%, and NH2: 5.7%, Supplementary Fig. 3). Additionally, the optical band gap of GQDs is 2.34 eV (Supplementary Fig. 4).

The photodynamic activity of N-GQDs was evaluated via radical trapping experiments (experimental details are provided in Methods). As shown in Fig. 1a, the 1O2 generating rate (r) of N-GQDs is 6.55 min–1 (25 °C, under 365 nm laser irradiation at 80 mW cm–2), which is higher than that of protoporphyrin (r = 6.45 min–1). Although the N-GQDs show a lower r than that of zinc protoporphyrin (r = 9.76 min–1, Fig. 1a), the above results demonstrate that N-GQDs can be used as a photosensitizer.

It is worth noting that the complicated sp2–sp3 carbon framework of N-GQDs makes it difficult to elucidate the photodynamic mechanism of N-GQDs 20. Therefore, the structural evolution of carbon frameworks based on rational structure descriptors is necessary. Inspired by a previous report 21, five key structural descriptors were selected for N-GQDs, including: (i) nitrogen dosage concentration, (ii) nitrogen configurations (N–(C)3, C–NH–C, and –NH2), (iii) oxygen content, (iv) oxygen functional groups (–OH, –COOH, and –CHO), and (v) particle size. A series of N-GQDs was prepared and characterized for structural evolution of carbon frameworks (see Supplementary Information for preparation details). Accordingly, three machine learning algorithms, including Random Forest (RF), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT), were then applied to analyze the relationships between these structural features (–NH2, C–NH–C, N–(C)3, –OH, –CHO, –COOH, and particle size) and the target (r). The comparison of the optimal models for grid search under three different machine learning algorithms indicates that the GBDT model exhibits optimal learning capability (Supplementary Fig. 5). Fig. 1b and 1c depict the coefficient of determination (R2) of the GBDT models for varying estimators (number of trees) and max tree depth on the training dataset through cross validation and test dataset, respectively. Usually, the model learns more details from the data set as the closer the value of R2 is to 1 with the augment of estimators. Nevertheless, higher R2 values may suggest the potential for overfitting of the model. Fig. 1d illustrates the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) score heatmap of the GBDT models performing on the test dataset. The greater accuracy of the model. Therefore, by comparing the model performance on the training and test datasets, the best GBDT model was determined by both estimators = 35 and max tree depth = 4. Typically, as the GBDT model comprises numerous trees, each tree holds a distinct decision-making process for the target solution. Fig. 1e shows a comprehensive visualization of one decision tree derived from the optimal GBDT model, displaying the structure, node-splitting conditions, sample distribution at each node, and the overall decision-making logic for data partitioning. More importantly, the Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) values of each feature indicate the contribution of these features to the target of the optimal model (Fig. 1f). Accordingly, the machine learning results thereby reveal that N–(C)3 performs the highest weight of 2.0998, indicating that it is a critical determinant of r. On the contrary, the –NH2 feature (0.0778), C–NH–C feature (0.0423), –OH feature (0.0075), –CHO feature (0.0417), –COOH feature (0.3545), and size feature (0.0415) with comparatively lower weights exert less influence on r. This provides definitive evidence of the relationship between the molecular structure of C3N QDs and their photosensitive activity. The N–(C)3 structure is deemed to be the critical structural factor for enhancing photodynamic catalysis. Therefore, it can be reasonably deduced that enhancement of the N–(C)3 structure within the C3N QDs will result in an improvement of the photodynamic activity of C3N QDs, thus achieving the optimal catalytic effect.

Based on the machine learning-driven structural evolution, the C3N QDs can be identified as the candidate photosensitizer with high photodynamic activity. As shown in Fig. 2a, both 1O2 and·OH were generated when C3N QDs were subjected to light irradiation. The r of C3N QDs is 27.32 min–1 at 25 °C (under 365 nm laser irradiation at 80 mW cm–2, Fig. 2b), which is much higher than that of traditional photosensitizers (protoporphyrin, r = 6.45 min–1; zinc protoporphyrin, r = 9.76 min–1). Moreover, C3N QDs also show a stable photodynamic activity (Δr < ± 2.5 min–1) in simulated cellular environment (include inorganic salts, biomolecules, proteins, and amino acids, Fig. 2c). However, the photodynamic activity of C3N QDs (r = 17.17 min–1 at 25 °C, under 365 nm laser irradiation at 80 mW cm–2) was significantly inhibited in the presence of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+, 1.0 nmol L–1, Fig. 2c and d). Fig. 2d shows the change in r of C3N QDs under different concentrations of NAD+. A jump in photodynamic activity can be observed. The r of C3N QDs reduced from 25.71 min–1 to 18.38 min–1 when the NAD+ concentration rose from 200 to 400 pmol L–1. Such a result indicates the potential interfacial transport between C3N QDs and NAD+. On the other hand, the changes in the photoluminescence intensity of C3N QDs under different concentrations of NAD+ (Supplementary Fig. 6 and 7) also support the above speculation. Importantly, the concentration range of NAD+ (Fig. 2d) in which the jump in photodynamic activity occurs is comparable to the cytoplasmic NAD+ concentration difference between normal cells and metabolically reprogrammed cells (Supplementary Fig. 8). Such a finding makes it possible to exploit the NAD+ concentration gradient in the cytoplasm of metabolically reprogrammed cells for targeted elimination.

To explore the interaction between C3N QDs and NAD+, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were employed to calculate the interaction energy at each step as C3N QDs and NAD+ approach each other. The results indicated that NAD+ was spontaneously adsorbed onto the C3N QDs (Fig. 2e). Furthermore, simulations of the charge transfer between C3N QDs and NAD+ revealed that when NAD+ is adsorbed on the C3N QDs, electron transfer occurs with 1.29 e (Fig. 2f). This indicates that the excited state of C3N QDs facilitates electron transfer to NAD+, which, in turn, hinders the formation of radicals by C3N QDs under light irradiation. Given that DFT calculations have confirmed the selective binding as well as the interfacial electron transfer between C3N QDs and NAD+, it is worth noting that such evidence is insufficient to elucidate the significant reduction in r of C3N QDs with the presence of NAD+. Such a situation possibly results from the focus on electron transport in the interfacial interaction instead of the proton transport during the DFT calculations. Therefore, the NMR relaxometry compatible with a light source 22-25 can be used to study the proton transport behavior of C3N QDs after the binding with NAD+. The longitudinal relaxation time (T1) measured by the 0.5 T NMR relaxometry is sensitive to the proton transport behavior, including the proton dissociation and transport 26,27. As shown in Fig. 2g, C3N QDs aqueous dispersion in a dark environment shows a T1 of 404.88 ± 6.80 ms, which is shorter than that of a 0.05-mmol L–1 Gd3+ aqueous solution 25, indicating the C3N QDs induce minor acceleration of the water proton exchange in a dark environment 28. After the addition of NAD+, the T1 slightly increased to 503.53 ± 23.05 ms, attributable to decreased proton dissociation at the C3N QDs’ interfacial and thus to moderate water proton exchange. When measuring the T1 with light induction (25 °C, under 365 nm laser irradiation at 80 mW cm–2), the T1 values of C3N QDs aqueous dispersion with and without the addition of NAD+ both decreased to 452.46 ± 8.28 and 179.18 ± 8.04 ms, respectively. Such a reduction in T1 after light irradiation on the aqueous sample represents the fact that irradiation by light may induce more dissociated protons at the interface of C3N QDs. Notably, with the addition of NAD+, the C3N QDs aqueous dispersion shows a long T1, originating from the binding of NAD+ with light induction and then suppressing the C3N QDs to produce more exchangeable protons, leading to the decrease in r.

It is worth noticing that in the highly complex intracellular environment, C3N QDs also show the selective interfacial transport behavior towards NAD+ (Fig. 2h). C3N QDs incubated with healthy cells in a dark environment show a T1 of 438.97 ± 15.42 ms. After the incubation with senescent cells, the T1 of C3N QDs slightly decreased to 247.80 ± 5.68 ms, attributing to the increased proton dissociation at the C3N QDs interface and thus the accelerated water proton exchange. When measuring T1 under light induction, the T1 values of C3N QDs incubated with healthy and senescent cells both decreased to 333.45 ± 14.21 and 84.78 ± 7.91 ms, respectively. Such a reduction in T1 after irradiation of the sample represents the fact that the light may induce more dissociated protons at the interface of C3N QDs. Notably, in senescent cells, the C3N QDs show the lowest T1 among the samples, originating from the low concentration of NAD+ in senescent cells under light irradiation, as the C3N QDs produce more exchangeable protons.

Thus, after uncovering the photodynamic activity of N-GQDs, the structural evolution of the carbon frameworks was achieved with the help of machine learning, and C3N QDs were proven to be efficient photosensitizers. Based on this, the selective interfacial transport behavior of C3N QDs towards NAD+ was further studied. After binding with NAD+, the interfacial charge transport characteristics and interfacial proton transport behavior of C3N QDs both changed significantly. This made C3N QDs show lower photosensitivity at high concentrations of NAD+. The interfacial transport behavior of C3N QDs was proven to persist in vitro.

In vitro interfacial transport of C3N QDs
The above results demonstrate the fluorescence response of C3N QDs to NAD+ and their varying photodynamic activities at different NAD+ expression levels. The feasibility of C3N QDs in identifying cells at different metabolic levels was further validated. A typical example is such that the concentration of NAD+ in the cytoplasm of senescent cells is lower than that of normal cells (Supplementary Fig. 8) 29. Indeed, C3N QDs exhibited expected results at both the cell and tissue levels (both in vitro cells and clinical tissue samples). Due to their ultrasmall size and appropriate ζ potential 30, C3N QDs are able to penetrate cells rapidly (3 h, Fig. 3a). It is noteworthy that the process of C3N QDs entering cells is not affected by the intracellular environment 31. This results in the same rate and amount of C3N QDs entering both normal and senescent cells (Fig. 3a). Additionally, C3N QDs can maintain the fluorescence activity within cells for 3–7 days (Fig. 3b and 3c, Supplementary Fig. 9).

Co-localization staining results indicate that after crossing the cell membrane, C3N QDs are mainly located in the cytoplasm and do not bind to specific organelles (Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, Supplementary Fig. 10). As shown in Fig. 3d, normal HUVECs transfected with red fluorescent protein (RFP, red dotted line) and senescent HUVECs, which were not transfected with RFP (blue dotted line), were mixed and cultured. In the normal HUVECs, bright cell fluorescence of C3N QDs was visible. In contrast, the fluorescence of C3N QDs in senescent HUVECs, characterized by lower NAD+ levels, was greatly weakened. At 72 h, the normal cells emitted both red and green fluorescence, while no significant green fluorescence was observed in the senescent cells within the same culture system. The sensitivity and specificity of the method with respect to identifying senescent cells were 93.43% and 93.08%, respectively (Fig. 3d, Supplementary Fig. 11).

Since a low level of cellular NAD+ in senescent cells is a common phenomenon 32, C3N QDs showed distinct fluorescence variations between senescent and normal cells in multiple cell type models of senescence induced by H2O2 or etoposide (ETO), including HUVEC, A549, bEND3, HK2, MRC5, and 3T3, as well as in primary cell models of replicative senescence (PEAC, PLF) (Supplementary Fig. 12–14). After C3N QDs were incubated with cells for 48 h, a significant difference in fluorescence intensity was observed between normal and senescent cells. Compared with normal cells, the fluorescence intensity of C3N QDs in senescent cells diminished by 44.6%, 49.9%, 56.3%, 64.3%, 46.9%, 58.6%, and 42.4%, respectively (Fig. 3e). The detection threshold for senescent cells based on the fluorescence intensity of C3N QDs was established at 90.0% (Fig. 3f, Supplementary Fig. 15).

The staining results of C3N QDs at the tissue level are consistent with the cell experiments. Due to their non-selective staining properties, C3N QDs are widely present in tissue samples. When examining the mouse aorta, C3N QDs were able to stain the entire layer of the blood vessel (intima, media, and adventitia) (Fig. 3g). In aorta samples from both young and senescent male mice, C3N QDs were different in the fluorescence intensity (Fig. 3h and 3i). Pulse wave velocity (PWV) can be used to assess arterial stiffness. The PWV of the aorta in senescent mice was significantly higher than that in normal mice (Supplementary Fig. 16). According to the analysis of receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, the sensitivity of C3N QDs was 96.0%, and its specificity was 72.0%, while the sensitivity of PWV was 68.8% and its specificity was 87.5%. Furthermore, the area under the curve (AUC) value of C3N QDs was 0.9552, which was significantly higher than the AUC value of PWV (0.7695), indicating that C3N QDs outperform PWV in terms of accuracy in detecting vascular aging (Fig. 3j). Furthermore, C3N QDs exhibited effective fluorescence selectivity across various organs in senescent mice, including the heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys (Fig. 3k, Supplementary Fig. 17).

C3N QDs can also be used to characterize aging in clinical samples. In clinical aortic vascular samples, the fluorescence intensity of C3N QDs in the aorta of young (20–45y) patients was significantly stronger than that of elderly (≥60y) patients (Fig. 4a and 4b, Supplementary Fig. 18). Similarly, the aortas from elderly patients showed vascular thickening and extensive aging across all layers. Clinical liver, kidney and skin samples demonstrated analogous results (Fig. 4c–4f, Supplementary Fig. 19–21). Notably, when using C3N QDs to stain skin samples from young and elderly patients, the dermis of elderly patients exhibited more obvious aging than the epidermis, suggesting that it is feasible to use C3N QDs to detect differences in aging at the tissue or cell level.

Statistics pertaining to clinical samples verified the negative correlation between C3N QDs intensity and aging (Fig. 4g). Compared to traditional aging assessment technologies that rely on NAD+ level detection (such as high-performance liquid chromatography, mass spectrometry, or enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) 33, the C3N QDs-based detection technique showed higher accuracy, the correlation analysis revealed a significant linear relationship between C3N QDs and NAD+ concentration (Pearson correlation coefficient = 0.7932, P < 0.0001), indicating that both variables exhibit a consistent trend in aging detection. (Fig. 4h, Supplementary Fig. 22). Furthermore, the AUC value of C3N QDs was 0.9305, significantly higher than that of PWV (0.9033), indicating that C3N QDs outperform PWV in terms of accuracy for aging detection (Fig. 4i).

In vitro interfacial transport for visual therapy
The results show that C3N QDs achieve the recognition of normal cells and senescent cells through the selective fluorescence response to NAD+. Concurrently, recognition of NAD+ by C3N QDs also causes changes in the photodynamic activity of C3N QDs, which makes it possible to eliminate senescent cells through the photodynamic activity of C3N QDs. Previous studies have shown that selective clearance of senescent cells (known as senolysis) in tissues helps to postpone aging 34. To demonstrate the efficacy of C3N QDs in the selective elimination of senescent cells, normal HUVECs and senescent HUVECs were co-incubated with C3N QDs (0.5 µg mL–1) for 3 h, and then irradiated by laser light with a wavelength of 365 nm at 80 mW cm–2 for 15 min, the mortality rate of normal cells was 0.33% ± 0.27% (Fig. 5a). In contrast, the lower NAD+ concentration of senescent cells caused C3N QDs to show higher photodynamic activity. The mortality rate of senescent cells after photodynamic therapy was 90.52% ± 4.23% (Fig. 5a, Supplementary Fig. 23). In addition, control experiments using identical irradiation parameters but without C3N QDs showed no significant impact on the viability of senescent HUVECs (Supplementary Fig. 24), confirming that the observed cytotoxicity arises from the photodynamic activity of C3N QDs rather than laser irradiation itself.

The heatmap can help understand how different treatments affect cellular mechanisms at the genetic level: S (senescence), S+C (senescence + C3N QDs), and S+C+I (senescence + C3N QDs + Irradiation). As depicted in Fig. 5b, within the S+C+I group, the expression levels of several aging-related genes changed notably. Specifically, the expression of genes such as MAPT, FOXO4, EPOR, FADS1, CTF1, and PTEN exhibited an upward trend, indicative of enhanced transcriptional activity or protein synthesis. In contrast, the levels of expression of other genes, namely FOS, NRG1, NOG, CXCL8, IL6, CTGF, CXCL1, SERPINE1, KLF4, MAP3K14, NGF, PLAUR, TRAF1, DDIT3, ARID5A, E2F1, TERT, and CEBPB, were found to be decreased in the S+C+I group. Analysis of molecular function highlights the prominent DNA-binding and transcriptional regulatory activities in the various experimental groups, with distinct changes seen in the S+C+I group (Supplementary Fig. 25–28). GSEA identified significant suppression of the KEGG p53 signaling pathway (NES = –2.16, FDR < 0.05) (Fig. 5c). These findings imply that the combination of C3N QDs and irradiation effectively scavenges senescent cells, leading to an improvement in aging-related conditions.

This reveals that C3N QDs can selectively recognize and clear senescent cells by leveraging variations in photodynamic activity. Indeed, C3N QDs showed consistent photodynamic therapy effects across various cell types, such as A549, bEND3, and HK2 (Supplementary Fig. 29–31). More importantly, the clearance of senescent cells led to significant changes in senescence markers such as p16, p21, and senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Quantitative analysis of β-gal across different cell lines unveiled that the β-gal levels in senescent cells treated with photodynamic therapy using C3N QDs reduced significantly, by 61.26% to 61.39% (Supplementary Fig. 32). In senescent cells treated with photodynamic therapy using C3N QDCs, a significant reduction in senescence markers was observed, decreasing by 26.07% to 87.43% (Fig. 5d–5f, Supplementary Fig. 33–34). At the same time, the cell proliferation ability of senescent HUVECs also changed accordingly. After the clearance of senescent cells, the proliferative capacity of the remaining cells improved 20.7% (Fig. 5g and 5h).

Experimental results at the cellular level validated the feasibility of using C3N QDs for the specific clearance of senescent cells. Further in vivo experiments, including those on the aorta, organs, and skin repair in induced senescence models, were conducted. The biosafety of C3N QDs was initially confirmed (Supplementary Fig. 35–37). Senescent mice induced by intraperitoneal injection of doxorubicin (10 mg kg–1) 35(Supplementary Fig. 38), followed by the administration of C3N QDs (5 μg mL–1, 100 μL) via the tail vein, and subsequent illumination of the aorta with 365 nm laser irradiation at 80 mW cm–2 for 15 min. The p21 staining revealed that p21 expression in the arteries of these doxorubicin-induced senescent mice significantly lowered after photodynamic therapy (Fig. 6a and 6b). Indeed, compared to the control group, senescent aorta treated with PDT showed 40.78% and 58.27% decreases in p21 and γ-H2AX expression, and an 85.69% increase in the Lamin B1 expression (Supplementary Fig. 39). This result was directly reflected in the reduction of vascular senescence (Supplementary Fig. 40).

Similar outcomes were observed in doxorubicin-induced senescence mouse models of the liver, spleen and kidneys (Fig. 6c–6f, Supplementary Fig. 41–43). In the liver, results were similar to those seen in the senescent vascular model, with β-gal levels reduced by 73.07% and p21 by 34.03%, and a 77.95% decrease in γ-H2AX expression (Fig. 6c and 6d, Supplementary Fig. 41). Importantly, in a liver fibrosis model associated with a high risk of tumorigenesis 36,37, C3N QDs also demonstrated satisfactory therapeutic effects, with reductions in β-gal by 87.6% and p21 by 64.30%, and a 64.2% reduction in γH2AX expression (Fig. 6e and 6f, Supplementary Fig. 44).

Finally, a practical and demonstrative application was conducted based on a diabetic skin injury model (Fig. 6g) 38,39. In this model, diabetic mice received C3N QDs (5 μg mL–1, 100 μL) through tail vein injection, followed by photodynamic treatment of the skin 365 nm laser irradiation at 80 mW cm–2 for 15 min). Similar to the senescence model, the tissue of the diabetic showed a lower NAD+ level 40,41, which made the healing rate of skin defects in the diabetic model significantly slower 42-44. Selectively eliminating cells with a low NAD+ expression in diabetic skin models is beneficial to the repair of skin defect models 43,45. In fact, after photodynamic treatment of C3N QDs, the skin injury model of diabetic mice showed better repair effects compared with the non-intervention experimental group. As illustrated in Fig. 6h, the control group exhibited significant inflammatory edema and scabbing between days 9–12. In contrast, the C3N QDs photodynamic therapy group experienced inflammatory edema from days 3–6 and scabbing from days 6–9. Moreover, wound healing via C3N QDs photodynamic therapy was noticeably faster than that in other groups, with the average relative area percentage of wound closure on day 12 being 84.98%, 85.1%, 84.83%, and 93.9% (Fig. 6i, Supplementary Fig. 45 and 46). HE staining results showed that after C3N QDs photodynamic treatment, the epidermis layer of the defective part of the skin was restored. On the day 12, the distances between the unhealed epidermal wounds were 2.35 mm, 2.28 mm, 2.21 mm, and 1.15 mm, respectively. Additionally, wound contraction and re-epithelialization were observed in the scar tissue (Fig. 6j–6m).
