## Methods

Ethical statement
All animal experiments were approved by the Animal Research Committee of Xinhua Hospital, Shanghai Jiaotong University School of Medicine (Ethical Approval No. [XHEC-F-2024-064]). All experiments involving human participants were approved by the Ethics Committee of Xinhua Hospital Affiliated to Shanghai Jiaotong University School of Medicine (Ethical Approval No. [XHEC-C-2024-145-1]). All human participants provided written informed consents, no compensation was provided.

N-GQDs fabrication
N-GQDs were prepared through hydrothermal reaction using m-phenylenediamine (m-PD, 99.5%, Aladdin Co., Ltd.) and pyrocatechol (Py, 99.5%, Aladdin Co., Ltd.). The detailed synthesis parameter of the hydrothermal treatment can be found in Supplementary Data 1. The reaction solution was filtered through a 0.02 µm alumina nano-porous membrane after the reaction was completed. The filtrate was then dialyzed using a 100–500 g mol–1 dialysis bag for 10 days. The dialysate was concentrated by rotary evaporation. When powder N-GQDs were needed, the concentrated dialysate was subjected to freeze-drying. The information of N-GQDs synthesis and characterization can be found in Supplementary Data 1.

C3N QDs fabrication
2,3-Diaminophenazine (DAP, 98%) was purchased from J&K Chemical Technology Co., Ltd (USA). 80.0 mL, 2.0 mmol L–1 of DAP aqueous solution was added to a 100 mL Hastelloy autoclave, heated and kept at 260 °C for 16 h. The product was filtered by a 0.02 µm alumina nano-porous membrane. Next, the obtained filtrate was dialyzed in a 3500 g mol–1 dialysis bag against deionized (DI) water for times to remove any unreacted molecules. The obtained reaction liquid can be directly used for biological experiments.

NMR relaxometry measurement
The T1 of sample was measured using a 0.5 T NMR relaxometry using inversion recovery (IR) sequence with the following parameters: spectrometer frequency = 21 MHz, π/2 pulse length = 6.52 μs, π pulse length = 13.04 μs, spectral width = 250 kHz, receiver gain 1 = 20, digital receiver gain 1 = 2, preamplifier gain = 3, time wait = 20000 ms, number of inversion times = 20, number of scans = 4. For T1 measurement with light induction, a 365 nm light source with an intensity of 80 mW cm–2 was applied to the sample.

Characterization techniques
The transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and high-resolution TEM were captured using JEM-ARM300F (JEOL Ltd.) operating at a voltage of 80 kV. The X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) spectra were obtained with an Escalab 250XIi (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc.). Ultraviolet-visible spectroscopy (UV-Vis, Cary 100 UV-Vis, Agilent Technologies, Inc.) was used to probe the UV-Vis absorbance of C3N QDs.

The dataset, derived from Radical_CAnalysis.xlsx, was preprocessed by selecting chemical features including –NH2, –NH, N–(C)3, OH, –CHO, –COOH, and size to predict the target variable r. To ensure the models mimic real-world predictive applications and strictly avoid data leakage, the data was randomly partitioned into independent training and testing sets prior to any model training or hyperparameter optimization. Predictive performance for the tree-based ensemble models, comprising Random Forest, XGBoost, and gradient boosting decision trees (GBDT), was evaluated using R2 and root mean square error score (RMSE) metrics. Furthermore, model interpretability was rigorously validated through SHAP analysis, Gini-based feature importance rankings, and individual decision tree visualizations to confirm that the underlying algorithmic logic aligns with chemical descriptors.

Machine learning methods
All the proposed methods were implemented using Jupyter Notebook 6.5.7 in Python 3.11.7 on a workstation with Intel® CoreTM i7 10700 CPU @ 2.90 GHz with 16 GB RAM and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 GPU with 12 GB memory.

Pearson correlation coefficient matrix calculation. The Pearson correlation coefficient measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two variables, X and Y. The coefficient value (r) ranges from –1 (perfect negative correlation) to +1 (perfect positive correlation). If 𝑟 is close to 1 or –1, it suggests a strong linear relationship, while values near 0 indicate a weak or no linear relationship. The Pearson correlation matrix is obtained by computing pairwise correlations between all features in a dataset, providing insights into their interrelationships and dependencies:
𝑟 = ∑𝑛𝑖=1(𝑥𝑖−𝑥̅)(𝑦𝑖−𝑦̅) / √∑𝑛𝑖=1(𝑥𝑖−𝑥̅)2 ∙∑𝑛𝑖=1(𝑦𝑖−𝑦̅)2 (1)
where 𝑥𝑖 and 𝑦𝑖 are the individual sample values of X and Y; 𝑥̅ and 𝑦̅ are the mean values of X and Y, respectively; and n is the number of data points in the dataset.

Principal component analysis. Principal component analysis (PCA) is a dimensionality reduction technique that transforms a high-dimensional dataset into a lower-dimensional space while preserving as much variance (information) as possible. Thus, PCA reduces the number of features while maintaining the essential structure of the data, facilitating easier visualization, interpretation, and further analysis. It works by identifying the directions (principal components) along which the data varies the most, then projecting the data onto these directions to reduce its dimensionality. The steps involved in PCA are:
(i) Covariance matrix calculation
The covariance matrix C represents how the variables in the dataset vary with respect to one another. For a dataset with features X1, X2, … , Xp, the covariance matrix is computed as:
C = 1/(n−1) (𝑋−𝑋̅)𝑇(𝑋−𝑋̅) (2)
where X is the data matrix (each column is a feature, and each row is a sample), 𝑋̅ is the mean-centered data (subtract the mean of each feature), n is the number of data samples.
(ii) Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
PCA calculates the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of the covariance matrix. The eigenvectors (principal components) represent the directions of maximum variance, and the eigenvalues indicate the magnitude of variance along those directions.
𝐶𝑣 = 𝜆𝑣 (3)
where v is an eigenvector (principal component), and 𝜆 is the corresponding eigenvalue.
(iii) Projection onto principal components
Once the eigenvectors are obtained, the data is projected onto the space defined by the first few eigenvectors, corresponding to the largest eigenvalues. This reduces the dimensionality of the data while retaining the maximum variance.
Z = X∙W (4)
where Z is the transformed data, and W is the matrix of eigenvectors (principal components).
Thus, PCA reduces the number of features while maintaining the essential structure of the data, facilitating easier visualization, interpretation, and further analysis.

Gradient boosting decision tree (GBDT). GBDT is an ensemble learning method that builds a strong predictive model by combining the outputs of multiple weak learners—typically shallow decision trees46. It employs a gradient descent approach in function space to optimize the model, particularly powerful for handling complex, nonlinear relationships in structured data 47. The steps involved in GBDT are:
(i) Model initialization with a constant prediction:
𝐹(𝑥) = argmin𝛾 ∑𝑛𝑖=1 𝐿(𝑦𝑖,𝛾) (5)
where 𝐹(𝑥) is the function that the goal is to learn, y is the true label, and x is the feature vector.
(ii) Iterative training (for m=1, 2, ..., M):
First, compute the negative gradients (residuals: 𝑟𝑖𝑚) for each sample:
𝑟𝑖𝑚 = −[𝜕𝐿(𝑦𝑖,𝐹(𝑥𝑖)) / 𝜕𝐹(𝑥𝑖)] 𝐹(𝑥)=𝐹𝑚−1 (𝑥) (6)
Second, for each leaf node 𝑅𝑗𝑚 (for j=1, ..., 𝐽𝑚), compute the optimal output value:
𝛾𝑗𝑚 = argmin𝛾 ∑𝑥𝑖∈𝑅𝑗𝑚 𝐿(𝑦𝑖,𝐹𝑚−1 (𝑥𝑖)+𝛾) (7)
Third, update the model by adding the new tree’s contribution:
𝐹𝑚 (𝑥) = 𝐹𝑚−1 (𝑥)+𝜂∑𝐽𝑚𝑗=1 𝛾𝑗𝑚 ⋅1{𝑥∈𝑅𝑗𝑚} (8)
where 𝜂 ∈ (0,1] is the learning rate controlling step size.
(iii) Loss functions:
For regression, mean squared error (MSE) is commonly used:
𝐿(𝑦,𝐹(𝑥)) = 1/2 (𝑦−𝐹(𝑥))2 (9)
For binary classification, logistic loss is frequently applied:
𝐿(𝑦,𝐹(𝑥)) = log(1+𝑒−2𝑦𝐹(𝑥)) (10)
The choice of loss function defines the direction of the gradient and affects how residuals are computed at each iteration.

Shapley additive explanations (SHAP). SHAP is an advanced model-agnostic interpretation framework based on cooperative game theory. It is designed to explain the output of any machine learning model by quantifying the contribution of each feature to an individual prediction 48. SHAP combines the consistency and local accuracy of additive feature attribution methods with the theoretical soundness of Shapley values from game theory.
(i) Mathematical definition:
Given a model f, an input instance x = {𝑥1, 𝑥2, ..., 𝑥𝑛}, and the set of all features N, the SHAP value 𝜙𝑖 for feature i is defined as:
𝜙𝑖 (𝑓,𝑥) = ∑𝑆⊆𝑁∖{𝑖} |𝑆|!(|𝑁|−|𝑆|−1)! / |𝑁|! [𝑓𝑆⋃{𝑖} (𝑥𝑆⋃{𝑖})−𝑓𝑆 (𝑥𝑆)] (11)
where S is a subset of the feature set excluding i, 𝑓𝑆 (𝑥𝑆) is the expected model output using only features in set S. The factorial term is a weighting factor ensuring fair contribution across all permutations.
(ii) Additivity and accuracy:
The sum of all feature contributions equals the difference between the prediction and the average model output:
𝑓(𝑥) = 𝐸[𝑓(𝑥)]+∑𝑛𝑖=1 𝜙𝑖 (12)

Cell culture conditions
All cell lines were cultured at 37 °C in a humidified 5% CO2 incubator. HUVEC (human umbilical vein endothelial cells) and primary lung fibroblasts (PLF, isolated from male rat lung tissues) were maintained in DMEM (Gibco, USA; Cat. No. C11995500BT) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Gibco, USA) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (P/S; Gibco, USA). Primary aortic endothelial cells (PAEC) were isolated from male rat aortic tissues and cultured in ECM medium (ScienCell, USA) with 20% FBS and 1% P/S. HK-2 cells (human renal proximal tubular epithelial cells) were grown in DMEM/F12 medium (Gibco, USA; Cat. No. C11330500BT) containing 10% FBS and 1% P/S. 3T3 (mouse embryonic fibroblasts), bEND3 (mouse brain endothelial cells), and MRC-5 (human lung fibroblasts) were propagated in standard DMEM (Gibco, USA) with 10% FBS and 1% P/S. A549 cells (Adenocarcinoma human alveolar basal epithelial cells) were cultured in F-12K medium (Gibco, USA) supplemented with 10% FBS and 1% P/S. All media were refreshed every 2–3 days, and cells were passaged using 0.25% trypsin-EDTA (Gibco, USA) upon reaching 80%–90% confluence. HUVEC (SCSP-5535), bEND3 (SCSP-5267), A549 (SCSP-503), HK-2 (SCSP-511), 3T3 (SCSP-5038), and MRC-5 (SCSP-5040) were obtained from the Cell Bank of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

Establishment of a cellular senescence model and identification of senescent cells
Hydrogen peroxide-induced cellular senescence model. The hydrogen peroxide-induced cellular senescence model was established by treating cultured cells with hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). Briefly, cells were cultured to 70%–80% confluence and then exposed to H2O2 (50 µmol L–1) for 4 h in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). Following treatment, cells were washed with PBS to remove excess H2O2 and allowed to recover in fresh medium for 72 h.

Etoposide-induced cellular senescence model. The etoposide-induced cellular senescence model was established by treating cultured cells with etoposide, a chemotherapeutic agent known to induce DNA damage and promote cellular senescence. Cells were plated at 70%–80% confluence and exposed to etoposide 2.5 µmol L–1 for 48 h in complete growth medium.

Replicative senescence model. To establish replicative senescence, cells were cultured in complete growth medium at 37°C with 5% CO₂ and serially passaged at a 1:4 split ratio upon reaching 80%–90% confluency. Proliferative capacity was monitored by calculating population doublings (PDs) using the formula:
PD = log(Final cell number / Initial cell number) / log2 (13)
Senescence onset was defined as a sustained < 0.5 PDs per passage for three consecutive passages.

Methods for senescent cell identification. Cellular senescence was verified using senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) staining, with senescent cells showing prominent blue staining under light microscopy. Additionally, changes in cell morphology, such as increased size and flattening, were observed. The expression of senescence markers, including p16, p21, and Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype (SASP), was further assessed by qPCR to confirm the senescent phenotype. Core SASP factors, including IL-1β, IL-6, CXCL1, CXCL14, CCL2, MMP-2, and MMP-9, were prioritized for their universal association with senescence-related inflammation and extracellular matrix remodeling.

Gene and protein expression analysis
qPCR-based gene expression analysis. Total RNA was extracted from cultured cells using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA), and cDNA was synthesized using a first-strand cDNA synthesis kit (Takara PrimeScript RT Master Mix, Takara Bio, Otsu, Japan) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Gene expression was quantified using real-time PCR with Hieff qPCR SYBR Green Master Mix (Yeason, Shanghai, Japan). Relative gene expression levels were calculated using the 2^−ΔΔCt method with GAPDH as the internal control. All primers were designed based on sequences retrieved from the NCBI Gene database and PrimerBank, with specificity verified using NCBI BLAST. Primers were synthesized by Shanghai Biotechnology Co., Ltd., and the sequences are listed in Supplementary Tables 1 and 2.

Protein extraction and western blotting. Total proteins were extracted from cells using RIPA lysis buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Beyotime, China). Protein concentrations were determined using a BCA Protein Assay Kit. Equal amounts of protein (20 μg) were loaded on 12% SDS-PAGE, separated at 100 V for 90 min, and then transferred onto 0.22 μm PVDF membranes (Millipore, USA) at 100 V for 60 min. The membranes were blocked with QuickBlock sealing solution (Beyotime, China) for 15 min at room temperature. Subsequently, membranes were incubated with primary antibodies (details and dilutions listed in Supplementary Table 3) overnight at 4°C. After washing with TBST (10 min, three times), the membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (Supplementary Table 3) for 1 h at room temperature. Protein bands were visualized using an ECL chemiluminescence detection system (Bio-Rad, USA) and quantified using ImageJ software. GAPDH was used as the internal loading control.

Co-cultured systems of normal and senescent HUVECs. Fluorescence images of a co-culture system comprising normal and senescent HUVECs. Senescent cells were pre-transfected with RFP prior to mixing with normal cells, and then the co-culture system was incubated with 0.5 μg mL⁻¹ C3N QDs for 72 h in 24-well plates.

Proliferation assays
Cell proliferation was assessed using two commonly employed methods: EdU (5-ethynyl-2’-deoxyuridine) labeling and CCK-8 (Cell Counting Kit-8) assay.

EdU assay. HUVECs were exposed to 10 μmol L–1 5-ethynyl-2’-deoxyuridine (EdU; Beyotime, Shanghai, China) for 2 h at 37 °C. Next, they were fixed, permeabilized, washed, and treated with 1× Apollo reaction cocktail for 30 min. Afterward, they were stained with DAPI (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) for 30 min. The HUVECs’ proliferation (ratio of EdU+ to all cells) was analyzed using images of randomly selected fields obtained on the fluorescence microscope (Olympus, Japan).

CCK-8 assay. Cells were plated in 96-well plates at a density of 5000 cells per well. After the indicated treatments for 24 h, 10 μL of CCK-8 reagent was added to each well and incubated for an additional 4 h at 37°C. The absorbance at 450 nm was then measured using a microplate reader. The relative cell viability was calculated as follows: (ODtreated – ODblank) / (ODcontrol – ODblank), where ODtreated, ODcontrol, and ODblank represent the absorbance of the treated samples, the untreated control samples, and the medium-only blank samples, respectively. For data analysis, the relative cell viability of the control group was set as 1.

NAD+ level detection
NAD+ levels were quantified using the NAD+/NADH Assay Kit (WST-8, Beyotime). Briefly, cells were plated at a density of 1 × 106 cells per well in 96-well plates. After appropriate treatment, 200 μL of lysis buffer was added to each well. Subsequently, 20 μL of the cell supernatant was mixed with 90 μL of alcohol dehydrogenase working solution and incubated at 37°C, shielded from light, for 10 min. Following this, 10 μL of chromogenic solution was added to each well, and the reaction was further incubated at 37 °C for 30 min in the dark. During this incubation, an orange-yellow formazan product was formed, and the absorbance was measured at 450 nm to determine NAD+ levels.

Subcellular localization of C3N QDs by fluorescence microscopy
To evaluate the co-localization of C3N QDs with intracellular organelles, HUVECs were incubated with C3N QDs (0.5 μg mL⁻¹) for 12 h. After washing with PBS, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100, and blocked with 5% BSA. Subcellular localization was analyzed through immunofluorescence staining as follows: Golgi apparatus: Labeled with rabbit anti-RCAS1 primary antibody (1:1000). Endoplasmic reticulum (ER): Stained with mouse anti-PDI primary antibody (1:400). Mitochondria: Targeted with rabbit anti-TOM20 primary antibody (1:200). Cytoskeleton: Actin filaments were labeled with Actin-Tracker Red-555 for 30 min. Nucleus: Counterstained with DAPI. Confocal imaging was performed using the GFP channel (488 nm excitation) for C3N QDs and the RFP channel (594 nm excitation) for organelle markers. Co-localization analysis was quantified using Pearson’s correlation coefficient in ImageJ.

Fluorescence intensity
Fluorescence intensity of C3N QDs in cell homogenates after incubation for different time points. Two groups of cells, normal and senescent, were cultured separately and incubated with C3N QDs (0.5 μg mL–1) for varying durations (1, 3, 6, 12, 24, and 48 hours). After the specified incubation periods, the cells were washed with PBS and counted to ensure equal cell concentrations. The cells were then homogenized, and the fluorescence intensity of C3N QDs in the homogenates was measured to evaluate the uptake and distribution of the nanoparticles in both normal and senescent cells at each time point. All units displayed as a. u. represent arbitrary units in this work.

PL emission intensity in co-cultured normal and senescent HUVECs. Normal and senescent HUVECs were co-cultured in 96-well plates at 5%, 10%, and 15% senescence ratios (e.g., 5% senescent + 95% normal, 10% senescent + 90% normal, etc.), with a total density of 5,000 cells per well. The co-culture system was incubated with C3N QDs (0.5 μg mL⁻¹) for 72 hours, followed by three PBS washes to remove unbound probes. PL emission intensity was quantified to evaluate senescence-dependent signal dynamics. The measurements were taken using a fluorescence spectrophotometer, with an excitation wavelength of 461 nm and an emission wavelength of 542 nm.

Quantification of PL emission intensity in blood samples using C3N QDs. The PL emission intensity in blood samples was quantified by incubating the samples with C3N QDs at a concentration of 5 μg mL–1 for 24 hours. PL intensity was measured using a microplate luminometer (LB 960, Berthold Technologies, Germany) configured with excitation and emission wavelengths of 461 nm and 542 nm, respectively.

Animal experiments
C57BL/6J male mice (species: Mus musculus) were obtained from Shanghai Jihui Laboratory Animal Care Co., Ltd. and housed at the Animal Facility of Xinhua Hospital. All male mice were 8 weeks old at the start of experiments and housed in a specific-pathogen-free (SPF) facility at Xinhua Hospital under a 12-h light/dark cycle with ad libitum access to standard chow and water. All procedures were performed to minimize animal suffering in compliance with the guidelines for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals.

Doxorubicin-induced senescence model. Senescence was induced in 8-week-old C57BL/6 mice by intraperitoneal injection of doxorubicin (10 mg kg–1) once daily for two consecutive days, followed by a 3-day observation period. Successful senescence induction was confirmed through staining for established senescence markers, including β-galactosidase, p21, and γ-H2AX.

Induction of liver fibrosis model. Liver fibrosis was induced in male C57BL/6 mice by intraperitoneal injection of 40% carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) solution (prepared by mixing CCl4 with olive oil at 4:6 volume ratio) at a dose of 1.5 mL kg–1 body weight, twice weekly for 7 consecutive weeks. Control mice received vehicle treatment. Successful fibrosis induction was confirmed by histological examination through hematoxylin and eosin (HE) staining and Masson’s trichrome staining.

Induction of a diabetic mouse model. Type 1 diabetes was induced in male C57BL/6 mice by a single intraperitoneal injection of streptozotocin (STZ, 200 mg kg–1 body weight). Control mice received vehicle treatment. After 9 days, fasting blood glucose levels were measured, and mice with glucose levels ≥ 16.7 mmol L–1 (≥ 300 mg dL–1) were considered successfully diabetic. After successful diabetes induction, dorsal hair was removed by shaving and depilatory cream to expose the skin. A full-thickness excisional wound (5 mm diameter) was created using a sterile biopsy punch. Wound healing progression was monitored every 3 days by digital photography, and the wound area was quantified using ImageJ software to calculate the healing rate. The unhealed wound distance was measured using a calibrated scale ruler. On day 12 post-wounding (before complete healing), mice were sacrificed, and skin tissues were harvested for histological analysis. For collagen quantification, sections were stained with Masson. High-resolution images of multiple tissue sections were captured under consistent microscopic conditions and analyzed using ImageJ software to quantify collagen deposition.

Measurement of aortic pulse wave velocity (PWV)
The mice were anesthetized by inserting an anesthetic mask into their mouths and noses, and anesthesia was maintained with isoflurane at a concentration of 1%–2% and a flow rate of 0.6–1.0 L min–1, and the heart rate of the mice was maintained at 400–650 bpm. Waveforms were captured at the aortic arch using a Vevo 2100 high-resolution small animal ultrasound machine, and then immediately measured at the descending aorta 35 mm distal to the aortic arch, and the PWV of mice was calculated using the formula D (m) / t (sec) to calculate aortic PWV in mice.
All measurements were repeated three times for averaging, with doxorubicin-induced senescence models serving as positive controls.

Photodynamic therapy
HUVEC were co-incubated with C3N QDs at a concentration of 0.5 μg mL–1 for 3 h. Following the incubation, the cells were treated with 365 nm laser irradiation at a power density of 80 mW cm–2 for 15 min to induce photodynamic therapy (PDT). After treatment, senescence-related markers, including SASP, β-gal staining, and the expression levels of p16 and p21, were assessed to evaluate the efficacy of the PDT treatment.

Mice were induced by intraperitoneal injection of doxorubicin (10 mg kg–1), followed by intravenous administration of C3N QDs at a concentration of 0.5 μg mL–1 in a volume of 50 μL via the tail vein. After the administration, the aorta was subjected to 365 nm laser irradiation at a power density of 80 mW cm–2 for 15 min to perform PDT.

Immunofluorescence and C3N QDs direct fluorescence staining
Following euthanasia via sodium pentobarbital (70 mg kg–1, intraperitoneal) combined with isoflurane inhalation, murine aortas, heart, liver, spleen, lung, and kidney tissues were harvested. Then, tissues were fixed in 4 % paraformaldehyde (24 h at 4 °C), and paraffin-embedded using standard protocols. Serial sections (5 μm thickness) were prepared for fluorescence-based analysis.

Antibody-based immunofluorescence staining. Standard immunofluorescence procedures were performed strictly according to the manufacturers’ instructions for specific protein markers. Details regarding the primary and secondary antibodies are summarized in Supplementary Table 3.

C3N QDs direct fluorescence staining. To assess the interaction of C3N QDs with tissues, an antibody-independent direct staining protocol was applied. Briefly, after deparaffinization and rehydration, tissue sections were blocked with 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA) for 30 min at room temperature. This blocking step was employed specifically to minimize the non-specific adsorption of the nanoparticles to the tissue matrix and the slide surface, thereby enhancing the signal-to-noise ratio. Subsequently, sections were incubated with C3N QDs (0.5 μg mL–1) for 30 min at room temperature, followed by three gentle washes with PBS to remove unbound QDs.

Image acquisition and quantification. All fluorescence images were acquired using an Olympus microscope. To ensure comparability, identical exposure times and acquisition settings were maintained across all groups. Quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensity was performed using ImageJ.

RNA sequencing
RNA sequencing was performed by Annoroad Gene Technology Company (Beijing, China). Total RNA was extracted from cultured cells (n = 3 biological replicates per group) using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA). mRNA was enriched using Oligo(dT) magnetic beads and fragmented prior to cDNA synthesis. Sequencing libraries were constructed following standard protocols and sequenced on an Illumina platform. Differential gene expression analysis was performed using the DESeq2 package, with genes showing an adjusted P value (Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate, FDR < 0.05) considered significantly differentially expressed. Heatmaps were generated to visualize expression patterns of differentially expressed genes. Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis was conducted using the clusterProfiler package, with terms showing P < 0.05 considered significantly enriched.

Human sample collection
Peripheral venous blood was collected from 90 hospitalized non-surgical patients using standard venipuncture procedures. Tissue samples (liver, kidney, aorta, and skin) were obtained from independent individuals during clinically indicated surgical procedures. Participants were stratified into two predefined age groups: young (20–45 years) and elderly (≥60 years). For each tissue type, samples were collected from 20 individuals per age group. Aggregated demographic characteristics, including age range, mean age, sex distribution, and sample numbers for each cohort, are provided in Supplementary Table 5. Although sex was recorded for all participants, no sex-stratified analyses were performed because the primary objective of the study was to investigate age-associated biological mechanisms.

Statistics and reproducibility
All statistical analyses were performed using Prism 10 (GraphPad Software Inc., USA). Data are presented as mean ± SD unless otherwise indicated. For comparisons between two groups, a two-tailed Student’s t-test was used. For comparisons between each experimental group and the control group, Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test was applied following one-way ANOVA. For comparisons among three or more groups, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s multiple comparisons post hoc test was applied. For factorial designs involving two independent variables, two-way ANOVA was performed, and simple main effects analysis was conducted to examine the effects of one factor at each level of the other factor. A P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All experiments were repeated independently at least three times with consistent results. The exact number of biological replicates (n) for each experiment is indicated in the corresponding figure legends. Representative images are selected from these independent replicates. No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. No data were excluded from the analyses.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript cannot be accepted for publication in any Journal. The quantum dots used for this study have not been characterized to any extent and there are huge flaws in the materials section. In addition, since no structural details are given for these CQDs, it is difficult to understand how the authors can claim the “structural evolution” in the title.
In general, the authors try to describe a strategy for the detection and treatment of senescent cells using quantum dots (C3N QDs). The authors used machine learning to define the structural properties of these carbon nanoparticles, specifically designed to have photodynamic activity. The paper explains how the QDs selectively interact with cellular environments based on NAD+ concentration, allowing for fluorescent detection of senescent cells (which have lower NAD+ levels) and targeted elimination through photodynamic therapy. The approach used is validated in vitro and in animal studies, demonstrating some potential for addressing aging-related pathologies. In addition, the interactions between C3N QDs and NAD+ have been studied using density functional theory (DFT) calculations, but there is nothing in the manuscript about how these calculations were performed.
Unfortunately, this work presents several inconsistencies, mainly concerning the material preparation and characterization. I believe that for the publication in any journal, several points should be carefully addressed and solved before considering the work.
In general the text is quite confusing and not scientifically acceptable. Other examples of nanodots or particles for the same scopes should be reported, to better describe the framework of interest for the materials prepared. Furthermore, the verb “decline” is used several times in the text in the sense of “decrease”. I don’t find it fitting the scientific context so I suggest substituting it with another verb. There are several assumptions not justified by the experiments.
Here is a list of aspects to be answered.
1) The synthesis reported in the supporting information does not match the one described in the text. Are the dots obtained from m-phenylenediamine and pyrocatechol or from 2,3-Diaminophenazine? Is the reaction done in autoclave? Have the nanoparticles been purified? These aspects should be corrected and clarified. Without the right description of the synthetic procedure, the characterizations reported lose some of their validity.
2) The authors should explain better the reason behind the choice of the two precursors. Assuming that m-phenylenediamine and pyrocatechol have been selected, as stated in the main text, how the two molecules are supposed to react with each other to form the carbon quantum dots? If the reactivity of the reagents is considered, it does not seem that they are chemically compatible (an aromatic amine and a phenolic compound). Is there any specific reason for the choice of those precursors? The nanoparticles synthesis should be better described to highlight the application sections.
3) As reported previously, (DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpcc.0c06996) m-phenylenediamine, and its structural isomers, are known for giving fluorescent side products that alter the emission properties of the final dots, ending up in imaginative results. In many cases, the use of m-phenylenediamine affords green emitting mixtures of low fluorescent carbonaceous particles and green emitting molecules. The emitting species absorb in the UV region of the spectra, close to 250 – 280 nm. Similar absorption band can be seen in the UV-spectra of the nanomaterials reported by the authors in Supplementary Figure 4. This aspect has strong implications in the reliability of the materials obtained. The authors should validate their material, by checking its composition, describe the right synthetic procedure and validate the absence of fluorescent impurities that may rule the nanomaterials fluorescence (or general properties). I suggest at least carrying out mass spectroscopy experiments, to evidence any molecular impurities.
4) In Supplementary Fig. 2 only one particle is shown for the HR-TEM. Anyway, the analysis of only one particle is not enough to define the overall crystallinity of the materials. Furthermore, crystallinity may arise from experimental conditions, such as the exposure of the nanoparticles to high voltage beam during the experiments. In other word, the crystallinity of only one particle cannot reflect the features of the bulk material. HR-TEM should be implemented with images of other nanoparticles and the morphological data should be supported with X-Ray diffraction on powder to confirm the nano- and bulk crystalline feature.
5) The purification of dots is a current topic in the scientific community (https://doi.org/10.1002/smll.202206714; 10.1039/C9NR01029G). Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy is a helpful technique to assess the purity and composition of the dots. In particular, molecular impurities appear in the spectrum as sharp peaks, peaks, while the protons of the nanoparticles give broad and enlarged signals (DOI: 10.1002/anie.202200038). Before any applications, the nanomaterials should be characterized by means of proton NMR spectroscopy and DOSY analysis to precisely describe their composition and the water diffusion coefficient (that should be lower than that of the precursors or small molecules in general) comparing the results with those of the precursors. The materials used for biological experiments should be exhaustively characterized. This is a golden rule in science.
6) Fluorescence is exploited for the quantum dots activity in vitro and in vivo. Anyway, only the UV-vis absorption spectrum is shown in the text, and no emission/fluorescence spectra are reported. Is it well known that carbon quantum dots should be characterized by a wavelength dependent fluorescence, otherwise the presence of fluorescent molecular impurities can be inferred. The authors should address this aspect.
7) For the photodynamic characterization, a laser emitting at 365 nm is selected. Anyway, in clinical applications- or biomedical publications- lasers at lower wavelength are used, since high energy sources can be cause of damage. This decreases a lot the interest for these materials in PDT.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript entitled “Structural evolution of carbon frameworks realizes in vitro interfacial transport in metabolically reprogrammed senescent cells for senolysis”, reported that nitrogen doping in graphene quantum dots (GQDs) is a factor determining their photodynamic properties, a conclusion supported by a machine learning model. The authors extend this finding to discuss the related photodynamic characteristics of C3N quantum dots (QDs). A key finding is that the fluorescence of C3N QDs taken up by cells changes depending on the intracellular NAD+ concentration, enabling the distinction between normal and senescent cells. Furthermore, the study challenged to reveals that subsequent laser irradiation endows these C3N QDs with senolytic activity.
While C3N QDs show potential as a senolysis, the in vivo experiments presented in Figure 6 lack a comparison between healthy controls and the senescence model. Additionally, the assessment of cellular senescence in the in vivo context is insufficient. Therefore, the establishment and validation of the cellular senescence models used throughout the manuscript require careful verification.
Regarding the diabetic ulcer model, the specific mouse model used is not described, and it is unclear whether the model was properly established. The lack of appropriate healthy controls precludes interpretation of the results of this study. Finally, the description of the cell lines used in various experiments is often unclear, making it difficult to assess the consistency and coherence of the experiments.
Detailed points regarding necessary revisions and additional data are listed below.
Major Comments

Reviewer #1 Comment 1: The synthesis reported in the supporting information does not match the one described in the text. Are the dots obtained from m-phenylenediamine and pyrocatechol or from 2,3-Diaminophenazine? Is the reaction done in autoclave? Have the nanoparticles been purified? Response: Thank the reviewer for pointing out the insufficient experimental procedures in this work. We have provided detailed experimental information, including the precursors, synthesis, and purification of nitrogen-doped graphene quantum dots (N-GQDs) and C N quantum dots (QDs).
This study is built upon the discovery of the photodynamic activity exhibited by N-GQDs. Leveraging machine learning techniques, we systematically guided the structural optimization of N-GQDs. The computational analysis ultimately identified that ordered nitrogen doping in GQDs, specifically C N QDs, yielded the most favorable performance. Consequently, this work involves two distinct types of GQDs, and there is full consistency between the synthetic procedures detailed in the supporting information and the descriptions provided in the main text. The N-GQDs with different structures were obtained through hydrothermal synthesis using m-phenylenediamine (m-PD) and pyrocatechol (Py), which describes in section 1.1 of the Supplementary Information. We modulated the doping amount and form of N atoms by varying the reaction time, temperature, and precursor ratio during synthesis. C N QDs were prepared from 2,3-diaminophenazin, and the preparation method is described in the section 1.2 of the Supplementary Information. The modulation of C N QDs and large-sized C N structures has been reported previously by us [Nat. Electron. 4, 486–494 (2021); Adv. Mater. 29, 1605625 (2017)].
Meanwhile, we fully understand the concerns raised by Reviewer 1 regarding the characterization results of N-GQDs. We believe these concerns are justified. Therefore, we have systematically supplemented the detailed preparation information of N-GQDs and the related characterization results in the revised Supplementary Information (Supplementary Table 1).
For the preparation of N-GQDs, the typical method is the hydrothermal reaction using m-phenylenediamine and pyrocatechol. The reaction solution was filtered through a 0.02 µm alumina nano-porous membrane after the reaction was completed. The filtrate was then dialyzed using a 100–500 g mol–1 dialysis bag for 10 days. The dialysate was concentrated by rotary evaporation. When powder N-GQDs were needed, the concentrated dialysate was subjected to freeze-drying. To confirm that the purified N-GQDs do not contain other small molecules or oligomers, we used thin-layer chromatography to confirm the purity of the product. No other impurities were found in the purified samples based on the thin-layer chromatography results.
It is worth noting that by adjusting the ratio of m-phenylenediamine and pyrocatechol, their concentrations, reaction time, and reaction temperature, the size and groups of N-GQDs can be modulated. The N-GQDs used for machine learning in Fig. 1 were prepared by modulating the above reaction conditions. Supplementary Table 1 lists the N-GQDs in Fig. 1, as well as the preparation conditions and characterization results for the N-GQDs used for machine learning. The characterization results include N and O contents based on XPS, group proportion analysis based on XPS, the average particle size of at least 100 of N-GQDs particles under TEM, the R value (Retention factor value) from thin-layer chromatography, the position of the main molecular ion peak (m/z) in MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry, and the 1O generating rate (r).

Response: Similar to the Reviewer #1 Comment 1, it is obvious that the Reviewer #1 misunderstood the preparation method of C N QDs. This led to the incorrect judgment. The preparation of C N QDs was obtained through hydrothermal synthesis from 2,3-diaminophenazine. Different structures of N-GQDs were prepared through hydrothermal synthesis from m-phenylenediamine and pyrocatechol, which are N-GQDs with disordered N atoms.
The preparation of C N from 2,3-diaminophenazine was first reported by us in 2017, and the detailed preparation mechanisms have been reported [Nat. Electron. 4, 486–494 (2021); Adv. Mater. 29, 1605625 (2017)].
Meanwhile, we understand the reviewer’s concern regarding the feasibility of the reaction between aromatic amines and phenols. In organic chemistry research, the coupling of phenols and aromatic amines is an important topic. For the coupling process in constructing N-GQDs, various metal-based catalysts have been developed. In recent studies, the coupling of aromatic amines and phenolic compounds under metal-free catalysis has also been reported [J. Am. Chem. Soc. 144, 1144–1151 (2022)]. It is worth noting that in organic chemistry research, researchers focus on high-yield and structurally clear small molecule coupling products. For example, the direct coupling of phenol and aniline results in diphenylamine. This makes it necessary to avoid the oxidation polymerization of phenols and aromatic amines during the reaction process. In contrast, the process of preparing GQDs by bottom-up synthesis has a basic reaction mechanism of small molecule coupling and carbonization. In fact, during the reaction process, the oligomers formed by the oxidation of phenols (especially in the solvent heating environment with air present) and the oligomers formed by aromatic amines can undergo coupling reactions. More importantly, the quinone structure formed by the oligomers of phenols at high temperatures can further promote the occurrence of the coupling reaction. This process has been clearly demonstrated in previous studies [J. Polym. Res. 27, 295 (2020); Synth. Met. 192, 66 (2014); J. Solid. State. Electrochem. 19, 2653 (2015); Russ. J. Gen. Chem. 87, 145 (2017)]. Fig. R1 presents the reaction mechanism proposed in previous studies.

On the other hand, NMR is a commonly used method for characterizing small molecule organic compounds and simple nanomaterials. However, in this case, NMR is not applicable for the characterization of N-GQDs. As the reviewer mentioned in the comment, the NMR spectra of nanoparticles are usually broad. This does not provide much help in clarifying the chemical environment of H and C atoms. In fact, in previous studies, NMR has shown importance only in the characterization of GQDs based on precise organic synthesis.
Finally, it should be emphasized that in all the preparation of N-GQDs, in order to confirm that the purified N-GQDs do not contain other small molecules or oligomers, we use thin-layer chromatography to confirm the purity of the product. Reviewer #1 Comment 6: Fluorescence is exploited for the quantum dots activity in vitro and in vivo. Anyway, only the UV-vis absorption spectrum is shown in the text, and no emission/fluorescence spectra are reported. Response: We understand the reviewer’s concern, but this concern is based on a misunderstanding of the QDs preparation in our work by the reviewer.
The reviewer mentioned that carbon dots or GQDs should have excitation wavelength-dependent properties and considered this property as the criterion for identifying carbon dots or GQDs. This is clearly incorrect. Excitation wavelength-dependent properties are characteristics of some carbon dots or GQDs, which are caused by their wide size distribution and rich surface fluorophores. There is still a lot of controversy over the mechanism of excitation wavelength dependence. This situation was well summarized in a review 9 years ago [Nanoscale 8, 7794–7807 (2016)].
It is worth noting that there are also carbon dots or GQDs that do not have excitation wavelength dependence. These QDs often have more defined surface structures and more uniform size distributions. Not only in our previous reports, but other researchers have also reported various carbon dots or GQDs that do not have excitation wavelength dependence. Here are some typical reports: Nat. Commun. 9, 2249 (2018); Adv. Mater. 29, 1605625 (2017); Sci. Adv. 6, eabb6772 (2020).
Furthermore, as we did in our response to Comment 1-5, we provided a series of characterizations for N-GQDs, N-GQDs-1 to N-GQDs-99. These characterizations include the synthesis conditions and analytical data for N-GQDs presented in Fig. 1, as well as those for the N-GQDs samples used in machine learning (N-GQDs-1 to N-GQDs-99). The characterization data encompass nitrogen and oxygen content determined by XPS, functional group ratio analysis from XPS, average particle size based on TEM imaging of at least 100 individual N-GQD particles, R values (retention factor) obtained from thin-layer chromatography, the m/z position of the main molecular ion peak in MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry, and the singlet oxygen generation rate (r). These characterization results are sufficient to prove that the product we prepared is N-GQDs rather than a polymer with fluorescence properties.
Reviewer #1 Comment 7: For the photodynamic characterization, a laser emitting at 365 nm is selected. Anyway, in clinical applications- or biomedical publications- lasers at lower wavelength are used, since high energy sources can be cause of damage. This decreases a lot the interest for these materials in PDT.
Response: Our focus lies in the structural evolution driven by machine learning and the interface characteristics of carbon nanomaterials. Although the short excitation wavelengths present the issues the reviewer mentioned, this does not affect the main points of this paper. It is obviously feasible to achieve photodynamic therapy in the red or near-infrared wavelength range in subsequent work.

Reviewer #2 Minor Comment 15: Page 15, Line 29, The manuscript claims, “Additionally, the dermis layer and hair follicles rapidly returned to normal.” This is a strong statement, as it is generally understood that severe dermal injury leads to scar formation, which replaces normal dermal structures, including hair follicles. Otherwise, please revise the statement to more accurately describe the observed histology, which likely involves wound contraction and re-epithelialization over a scar.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We have revised the statement on page 15, line 29 (lines 31–32 in revised manuscript) to more accurately reflect the observed histology. The text now reads: “Additionally, wound contraction and re-epithelialization were observed in the scar tissue”. This modification better aligns with the typical wound healing process involving scar formation rather than complete regeneration.
